title: On septic in Sebastian? How to find your tank, when to pump it, and the signs of trouble
seoTitle: Sebastian Septic Tank Care: Pumping, Records, Warning Signs
description: Sebastian septic owners: how to pull up your tank's permit and site plan for free, how often to pump, what never to flush, and the warning signs to watch.
dek: Sewer may be years away for many Sebastian streets. Until then, the septic tank in your yard has to keep working. Here is how to find it, care for it, and spot trouble early.
facebook: Do you know where your septic tank actually is? Or when it was last pumped? Here's how to pull up your tank's records for free, how often to pump, and the warning signs to watch for.
keywords: how often to pump septic tank Florida

body.text: If your Sebastian home is on septic, you have probably heard plenty lately about sewer and the 2030 deadline. That is a big question for later. Here is a smaller one for now: is the tank in your yard in good shape?
A septic system mostly works out of sight. That is why it gets forgotten. The good news is that keeping it healthy is not complicated, and the records for your system are free to look up.

body.title: The short version
body.text: Florida's Department of Environmental Protection says to have your tank inspected and pumped every 3 to 5 years by a state-licensed septage service. Flush only human waste and toilet paper. Keep cars, trees and roof water off the drainfield. You can look up your system's permit records for free at SepticSearch.com, and septic permits in Indian River County still go through the Florida Department of Health office, 772-794-7440.
Step one: find your tank and drainfield
You cannot protect what you cannot find. The state's septic owner's guide says to know where your drainfield is, so you do not park on it, dig in it or plant over it.

In Indian River County, septic and well records are online for free. The Florida Department of Health in Indian River County runs an Online Septic Search at SepticSearch.com. Pick Indian River County, choose Records Search, and look up your address or the parcel ID from the Property Appraiser. Then click View History to see what is on file.

Records can include the application, permit, site evaluation, inspections and any repair permits. For permits issued after Jan. 1, 2000, the county health office has scanned site plans, which show where the system was put. If your home is older, you may only see part of the history, but it is still worth a look.
How often to pump

The Florida Department of Environmental Protection's owner's guide says to have the tank inspected and pumped every 3 to 5 years by a state-licensed septage disposal service. The University of Florida's IFAS extension gives the same 3-to-5-year rule. It notes that the right timing depends on how many people live in the home, the size of the tank and how much water you use.
Why it matters: solids build up in the tank over time. If they get too high, or a filter clogs, the system can fail. A failed drainfield is a much bigger job than a pump-out.
What goes down the drain, and what never should
Your tank depends on helpful bacteria to break down waste. A few habits keep them working:

items: Flush only human waste and toilet paper. "Flushable" wipes and kitty litter can clog or damage the system.
Do not pour cooking oil or grease down the drain.
Do not pour strong chemicals, cleansers or old medicines down drains or toilets. They can kill the bacteria.
Use the garbage disposal sparingly, or not at all. If you use one, have the tank checked more often.
Fix leaky faucets and running toilets. Every extra gallon goes through the tank.
Spread laundry out over the week instead of doing it all in one day.

body.text: Take care of the drainfield
The drainfield is the part of the system that does the final cleaning in the soil. It needs air and room to work. The state and UF/IFAS both list the same basics:

items: Do not drive or park cars, trucks or heavy equipment on it.
Plant only grass over and near it. Tree and shrub roots can clog the pipes.
Point gutters and downspouts away from the tank and drainfield.
Do not cover any part of the drainfield, for example with a slab or a shed, without a permit.
Keep water softener backwash at least 15 feet away from the tank and drainfield.

body.text: Warning signs to watch for
Call a licensed professional right away if you notice any of these:

items: Sewage backing up into the house or onto the yard.
A sewage smell from drains, or around the tank or drainfield.
Sinks, tubs and showers that drain slowly.
Standing water, or soggy, spongy ground over the tank or drainfield.

body.text: Who handles septic permits here

Florida moved much of its septic program to the Department of Environmental Protection, which has enforced the state's septic rules since July 1, 2021. But permitting moved to DEP in only 16 counties, mostly in the Panhandle, and Indian River County is not one of them. Here, septic permits and inspections still go through the Florida Department of Health in Indian River County, Environmental Health, 1900 27th St., Vero Beach, 772-794-7440.

As for sewer: under the 2023 state law, homes on lots under 10 acres must connect to sewer where it is available, or switch to an enhanced septic system that cuts nitrogen by at least 65%, by July 1, 2030. Indian River County is working on North Sebastian Phase 3, and it is working with Sebastian's Community Redevelopment Agency on sewer for some businesses and residents. Until sewer reaches your street, good septic care is what keeps your system running.
What to do

items: Look up your address on SepticSearch.com and save or print your septic permit and site plan.
Find the last time your tank was pumped. If you do not know, or it has been more than 3 to 5 years, have it inspected and pumped by a state-licensed septage service.
Walk the yard and mark where the drainfield is. Keep cars, trailers and new trees off it.
Check that gutters and downspouts drain away from the tank and drainfield.
Post a note by the sink: only human waste and toilet paper, no grease, no wipes.
Questions about permits or records? Call the Department of Health in Indian River County at 772-794-7440.

faq.q: How often should I pump my septic tank in Florida?
faq.a: The Florida Department of Environmental Protection says every 3 to 5 years, by a state-licensed septage disposal service. Homes with more people, a smaller tank or a garbage disposal may need it sooner.

faq.q: How do I find my septic tank records in Indian River County?
faq.a: Use the free Online Septic Search at SepticSearch.com. Choose Indian River County, search by address or parcel ID, and click View History. Scanned site plans are available for permits issued after Jan. 1, 2000.

faq.q: Who issues septic permits in Sebastian FL?
faq.a: The Florida Department of Health in Indian River County, Environmental Health, 1900 27th St., Vero Beach, 772-794-7440. Indian River County is not one of the 16 counties where DEP took over septic permitting.

faq.q: What are the signs of a failing septic system?
faq.a: Sewage backing up into the house or yard, sewage smells, slow-draining sinks, tubs and showers, and standing water or spongy ground over the tank or drainfield.

faq.q: Can I park or build over my drainfield?
faq.a: No. Do not drive or park on it, and do not cover any part of it without a permit. Plant only grass over it.
